newsitem.title: USA: Olympics organizers predict slight budget surplus.
newsitem.headline: Olympics organizers predict slight budget surplus.

text.p: Atlanta Olympics organisers, aided by greater-than-expected souvenir sales, said on Tuesday they expected to end next year with a surplus of just under $10 million.

"We can say for certain that we raised more money than we spent," said A.D. Frazier, chief operating officer for the Atlanta Committee for the Olympic Games (ACOG). He said final payments for television rights, licensing and other revenues were expected to trickle in during 1997.

"The financial obligations that we have to meet ... (are) less than the amount of money we have in hand or are going to have by the end of the summer," Frazier said. "We didn't leave very much money on the table."
Officials would not predict ACOG's final profit, but committee president Billy Payne said it would be less than $10 million.

"We did not put a number on the amount of money that would be left at the end when our work is complete mid-summer, because we still have a significant amount of work to do in construction and retrofit and a significant amount of money yet to collect," Payne said. "Any numbers ... are only speculation."
Income from sales of Olympic memorabilia have so far totalled $7.5 million, ACOG said, about twice the amount that was budgeted.

Frazier said the books on ACOG's $1.71 billion budget will not be closed until next year, after Atlanta Fulton-County Stadium is demolished and replaced with a paved parking lot. A fraction of the budget surplus will be offered to the Atlanta city government foundation for a possible Olympic Museum, Payne said.
Organisers faced an "amazingly small number" of lawsuits after the Summer Games, Payne said. Still pending is a lawsuit that challenged the way some ticket packages were priced.
"We have a number of cases in litigation," he said. "We have amazingly few personal injury cases. We have ongoing litigation with designers of the stadium."

He said ACOG faces no lawsuits from disgruntled street vendors who complained about the way city officials treated them. All of the pending lawsuits are fully covered by insurance or are "reserved for potential recovery in our budget," Payne said.
